To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the heat shock response is a key component of thermal radiosensitization and that it is a key component in thermal radiosensitizers.

(a) the heat shock response (HSR) is a major determinant of tumour response to heat and radiation, and (b) the HSR is a major determinant in the development of heat-induced tumour cell radioresistance.

1) heat sensitizes tumours to radiation, 2) the optimal temperatures are in the range 40–42°C, 3) the optimal fractionation schemes are based upon avoidance of the development of thermal tolerance, and 4) the optimal times for heat administration are immediately before or during the administration of ionizing radiations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an integrated model for predicting and controlling heat-induced tumour responses.
the elucidation of the molecular basis of heat sensitivity, heat tolerance development, and the heat shock response.
the development of a new paradigm for combined hyperthermia and radiation therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a heat shock response, induced in a variety of ways, is likely to be a major component of the future of cancer therapy.
the heat shock response is an important component of the radiation biology of cancer therapy.
heat sensitivity is not an absolute property of a given tumour, but a relative one that is determined by the interaction of many factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the heat shock response (HSR) plays a central role in the development of thermal tolerance.
the heat shock response is an essential component of the heat response.

heat sensitivity is a function of the temperature, the rate at which it is applied and the rate at which the temperature is reduced, as well as the time at the elevated temperature, and the duration of the exposure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of hyperthermia to improve the outcome of radiation therapy requires a rethinking of the basic concepts of the heat shock response and its relationship to tumour reoceanation.
heat is a potent radiosensitizer.
the heat shock response is not a single phenomenon but rather a collection of diverse and complex responses.
